studies.Title: Incidence of cancer and mortality following alpha-tocopherol and beta-carotene supplementation: a postintervention follow-up.
studies.Reference: Incidence of cancer and mortality following alpha-tocopherol and beta-carotene supplementation: a postintervention follow-up.
studies.Timing: 6-year postintervention follow-up after 5 to 8 years of supplementation

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: Postintervention follow-up assessment of cancer incidence and cause-specific mortality (6 years [May 1, 1993-April 30, 1999]) and total mortality (8 years [May 1, 1993-April 30, 2001]) of 25 563 men.
extraction_supporting_text.cases: For prostate cancer incidence (n = 672), the RR was 0.88 (95% CI, 0.76-1.03) for participants receiving alpha-tocopherol compared with nonrecipients.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: Overall posttrial relative risk (RR) for lung cancer incidence (n = 1037) was 1.06 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.94-1.20) among recipients of beta-carotene compared with nonrecipients. For prostate cancer incidence (n = 672), the RR was 0.88 (95% CI, 0.76-1.03) for participants receiving alpha-tocopherol compared with nonrecipients.
extraction_supporting_text.confidence_interval: For prostate cancer incidence (n = 672), the RR was 0.88 (95% CI, 0.76-1.03) for participants receiving alpha-tocopherol compared with nonrecipients.
extraction_supporting_text.comparison: for participants receiving alpha-tocopherol compared with nonrecipients
extraction_supporting_text.design: In the ATBC Study, 29 133 male smokers aged 50 to 69 years received alpha-tocopherol (50 mg), beta-carotene (20 mg), both agents, or placebo daily for 5 to 8 years.
extraction_supporting_text.timing: Postintervention follow-up assessment of cancer incidence and cause-specific mortality (6 years [May 1, 1993-April 30, 1999])

headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 2 studies yielded an effect size of 1.18 (95% CI: 0.95–1.46), indicating no statistically significant association between antioxidants and prostate cancer. Although the point estimate suggests a potential positive relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by substantial heterogeneity (I² = 60.98%), reflecting considerable variability across studies.
